ca_cracked_towers.blurb: Cracked Towers is a small cliff in the upper part of Owens River Gorge near Bishop, in the Eastern Sierra, at roughly 5,700 feet. Two freestanding towers, one of them a smooth pink slab, stand in front of a taller wall above a marshy flat. Of its 14 routes, about two thirds are bolted and the rest are trad. The grades spread widely: a few moderates from 5.7 to 5.9, several 5.10s, a hard core of 5.12s, and a single 5.13. A couple of the longer lines go in two pitches. The gorge walls face a mix of directions, so you can usually pick sun or shade.
ca_cracked_towers.parking_note: Use the Upper Gorge parking lot, then start down the upper power plant road on foot.
ca_cracked_towers.approach: Walk the power plant road for a couple of minutes, then descend the steep trail into the rocky gully, which is marked by a big cairn. At the bottom take the left-hand trail, keeping the talus slope on your left, to a telephone pole chained in place above the swampy ground.

ca_5_13.blurb: A remote limestone crag above Hayfork in Northwest California, at about 3,400 feet. The name is a joke about the old bushwhack to reach it, not about the grades: the 14 routes run from 5.7 up to a handful of 5.13s, nearly all of them bolted with a single trad line. Roughly half fall in the 5.12 to 5.13 range, so it suits strong sport climbers. The wall faces east to north, which keeps it shaded on hot inland days, though early in the season it can hold snow and seepage. A trail now makes the walk about 15 to 20 minutes, and it works best as an overnight trip.

ca_upper_tier_12.blurb: Upper Tier is the higher of the two walls of the Public Sanitation Wall, on the south side of Yosemite Valley at about 4,400 feet. It has 14 routes on steep, clean rock, ten bolted and four trad. There is nothing truly easy: two at 5.10, seven at 5.11 and five at 5.12, so it is a spot for climbers already comfortable leading in the 5.10s who want sustained face climbing. The approach is short but involves a talus slope and a scramble, and the walk to the base from the road is quick.
ca_upper_tier_12.approach: Hike up the talus slope toward the Lower Tier, then pick up the trail that scrambles uphill on its left side to reach the upper wall.

ca_arid_piles_northwest_face.blurb: This is one face of the Arid Piles formation, in the Lost Horse area of Joshua Tree National Park at about 4,100 feet. The climbing is mostly trad, with a mix of cracks and faces, plus a pair of top-rope lines. The 14 routes include one easy outing, a core of seven in the 5.10s, four at 5.11 and two at 5.12. Many were put up in a bold 1980s style, so expect serious leads on granodiorite. The face is shaded in the morning and catches the sun in the afternoon.
ca_arid_piles_northwest_face.approach: Start at the Real Hidden Valley lot and follow the climbers' trail west, passing the formations along the way, until you reach the south end of the Lost Horse area where the Arid Piles stand.

ca_back_wall.blurb: Back Wall is a sandstone wall at Stoney Point, the historic city-park crag in the San Fernando Valley north of Los Angeles. It is mainly a top-rope wall: eleven of its 14 climbs are top ropes, with one trad line and two boulder problems. The grades run from an easy chimney through several routes in the 5.9 to 5.10 range, with a few 5.12s and boulder problems at V1 and V5. Rock quality varies and the wall tends to be uncrowded. It is sunny in the morning and likely shaded late in the day. A beehive sits mid-wall, so go early. The sandstone is fragile when wet.

ca_c_left_of_the_roof.blurb: Left of the Roof is a sport sector of Riverside Quarry in the Inland Empire, set between the Metro Sector and the Roof Area. All 14 routes are bolted, and it favors strong climbers: one 5.10, three 5.11s and ten at 5.12. The quarry granite is high quality, with a few holds altered by old quarrying work. The quarry as a whole faces mostly west, so summer sessions are best in the morning. Many lines here are long enough that a 70 meter rope is needed to lower off safely.

ca_upper_crust.blurb: Upper Crust is a wall on the East Side of Pinnacles National Park, in the Central Coast region at around 1,900 feet. The breccia is good quality, and the wall stays in shade all day, which makes it a pleasant warm-weather choice with fewer people. Twelve of its 14 routes are bolted and two are trad. The range is wide, from 5.5 up to a 5.12, with 5.10 the biggest group and several easier lines that suit newer leaders. Most are well protected, and the routes are also easy to top rope.
